1:
Keil and Delitzsch set out the whole design before anything is expounded. Samaria and Jerusalem, as the capitals and representatives of the two kingdoms, are two sisters who have practised whoredom from the days of Egypt onward; Samaria carried it on with Assyria and Egypt and was given up into the power of the Assyrians for it; Jerusalem, instead of taking warning, played the harlot still more grievously with Assyria and the Chaldeans and at last with Egypt again, so that the Chaldeans will make war upon her and she will experience in full the fate of her sister; then both kingdoms are shown once more, in severer terms, the guilt of their idolatry, and punishment for adultery and murder alike is foretold. Gill notes only that this is another prophecy on the same subject, and Clarke that the idolatries of the two cities are figured by the practices of two common harlots, the same metaphor being enlarged in an earlier chapter, since the aim of the prophet is to excite the utmost detestation of the crime.

Henry begins with the repetition. God had spoken to this effect often, and speaks the same thing once, yea twice, yea many a time, and all of it little enough, since man does not perceive it; to convince sinners of the evil of sin there is need of line upon line, so loth are we to know the worst of ourselves. He then draws out what the choice of figure implies. That the sins most provoking to God should be represented by the sin of whoredom plainly intimates what an exceedingly sinful thing uncleanness is, since it is itself among the worst of sins and the worst of other sins are compared to it; from which he presses a greater detestation of all fleshly lusts, as warring against the soul, alienating the mind from God and all that is good, debauching conscience and rendering men odious in the eyes of a holy God.

The two sisters are identified without dispute. Henry and Clarke both trace the division from a single people, Henry noting that the kingdom of Solomon was so populous that immediately upon his death it divided in two, and Clarke that all were derived from one source until the schism, after which the ten tribes and a half separated from Judah and Benjamin and became two peoples under different kings, called sisters because of their consanguinity. Gill and Wesley identify them as the ten tribes and the two. On the shared beginning in Egypt, Gill has them learn and practise the idolatries of the land while they sojourned there as strangers and were still one body, and Wesley glosses the whoredoms in a word as idolatry.

The names carry the argument. Gill, Ellicott and Wesley agree that the elder sister is so called for size rather than age, Ellicott saying outright that the word should be translated greater, and Gill that the ten tribes were more in number than Judah and greater in power and riches. All three read the first name as her own tabernacle, Ellicott because she set up her own worship instead of resorting to the Temple, Wesley because falling off from the house of David she fell off from the tabernacle of God, and Gill because her worship and her places of worship were of her own appointing, namely the calves at Dan and Bethel. The second name they read as my tabernacle is in her, since the southern kingdom still contained the sanctuary of the Lord. Wesley adds that they were his by solemn marriage covenant, and that the sons and daughters they bore were an increase in numbers among whom some were children of God by faith and obedience.
5:
Clarke pauses over the manner of the chapter before expounding it. A parallel is run between idolatry and prostitution, and the circumstances of the latter illustrate the peculiarities of the former, which is why the chapter carries so many of what we should call indelicate expressions; in such cases, he suggests, perhaps the matter alone was given to the prophet and he was left to use his own language. He compares the prophet among the Jews to Juvenal among the Romans, a rough reprover of the most abominable vices, both speaking of things as they found them, stripping vice naked and scourging it publicly, and he warns that the original is rougher still than the translation. There are a few things here in the shade, he adds, that might be illustrated by anatomy, and it would not be difficult to do it, but they are not necessary to salvation and he will not take off the covering, since they were sufficiently understood by those for whom they were designed.

Gill offers three renderings of the clause that fixes the offence. She played the harlot while she was his married wife, who ought to have cleaved to him alone; or under him, under his cover and protection, so that it was her interest to serve him only; or, as the Syriac has it, besides him, worshipping other gods in the room of the true God or alongside him. Wesley reads it the same way, that she was his when under his government and protection.

The lovers are described and placed. Ellicott presses the word rendered neighbours, which he would give as drawing near, and insists the nearness is not local but spiritual, a sympathy in idolatry, since the same people are described later as coming from far; he grants that little record remains of the earlier connection, though tribute exacted of one king seems to imply an earlier intercourse and the Assyrian records make another tributary, and he thinks the name is used broadly enough for the whole northern power in contrast to Egypt on the south. Gill and Clarke both dwell on the clothing, Gill noting that the colour was one the Assyrians were fond of and put upon their soldiers, taking to the eye, and mentioned because men finely arrayed are more engaging to women who are fond of dress, and Clarke that the purple dye was highly valued among the ancients and used at first only by kings and afterwards by officers of high rank. Ellicott adds that the Assyrians, like the Egyptians, made large use of cavalry as a warlike nation required, which is why the multiplication of horses had been forbidden to the people, and Wesley that they were skilful riders well furnished with choice horses.

The old idolatry is not given up with the new. Gill observes that though they took in the gods of the Assyrians they did not relinquish the golden calves at Dan and Bethel, made in imitation of Egyptian deities whose worship they had learned in Egypt, and Ellicott that at the mention of their idols the reality breaks through the figure and leaves no doubt of the meaning of the allegory. On the sentence, Gill has the delivering into the hand of her lovers reach persons, families, riches and the kingdom itself, and Wesley names the king under whom the northern kingdom was utterly destroyed and the conqueror who executed it. Ellicott corrects the last word, that where she is said to have become famous a better rendering would be notorious, the conquest of the city and the captivity of the northern tribes having by then been accomplished more than a century and a quarter and made them a byword among the nations.
11:
The younger sister had every reason to do better. Henry recalls that Hosea observed the two tribes retaining their integrity in great measure while the ten had apostatized, and that this was justly expected of them; but it did not last. Unhappy matches between the house of David and the house of Ahab had brought the worship of Baal into the southern kingdom, and the reforming kings had worked it out again, so that at the time of the captivity of the ten tribes, in the reign of Hezekiah, things stood in a good posture. Under Manasseh, soon after the south had watched the destruction of the north, they became more corrupt than the north had been. Henry presses the perversity: instead of being bettered by the warning that destruction gave them they were made worse, as if displeased that the Lord had made that breach upon their sister and therefore disaffected to his service, and instead of standing in awe of a jealous God they grew strange to him and liked better those gods that would admit of partners. Those may justly expect the judgments of God upon themselves, he concludes, who take no warning by his judgments upon others, and who see in others what the end of sin is and still make a light matter of it. Gill states the failure briefly, that when the two tribes saw the idolatries of the ten and the destruction that followed, they received no instruction from it.

Ellicott makes the comparison exact. Enough having been said of the elder to form a basis for it, the prophet turns to the younger, whose idolatries exceeded her sister not comparatively only but actually, as the account of the reign of Manasseh shows; and besides her connection with Assyria she made alliances with Chaldea and intrigued with Egypt and others. Gill fixes one such dealing in the reign of Ahaz, who sent to the king of Assyria for help and took from there the pattern of an altar, had one built like it at Jerusalem and offered upon it. Ellicott adds why the Assyrian warriors are so attractively drawn: engagingly, to carry out the figure, and as very powerful, to explain the political attraction, the people being at once fascinated by their splendour and overawed by their power.

The portraits on the wall get a careful note. Ellicott observes that such portraitures, with evidence that they were once executed in brilliant colours, are characteristic of both Egypt and Assyria, where stone for sculpture abounded, and that given the close connection in race and custom between the Assyrians and Babylonians there can be no doubt the same portraitures were common on the more perishable brick of the latter, who are the people in view here. The monuments, he says, concur in representing the warriors of Assyria and Babylonia as delighting in extreme gorgeousness of apparel, though it is difficult to render each particular of their dress accurately into English. He adds that the exiles the prophet addressed were familiar with these pictures, so his way of speaking of them mattered for checking any disposition to fall into idolatry through them.

The dress itself is read two ways. Gill takes the girdles for a token of dignity and authority, the peculiar custom of the Babylonians as Kimchi observes from the Talmudists, and the head covering for turbans of various colours after the manner of the Persians. Wesley makes them military instead, soldiers belts standing for the rest of the habit of a soldier, with attire rich, comely, large and of divers colours, and men of princely aspect and majesty. Gill notes the plain sense running under the figure, that the increase of her whoredoms was an increase in the number of her idols, in which she outdid her sister, and that the defilement seen was defilement with idols.
16:
The seeing is not confined to sight. Ellicott takes it widely enough to cover knowledge obtained in any way, since the intercourse between the two lands was so close that many had seen the Babylonians in person while others knew of them by report. Gill keeps the figure, that as lustful women fall in love with the pictures of men, so a vehement desire after the idols of the Chaldeans prevailed upon the sight of their images. On the sending of messengers Ellicott gathers the record: one king sent messengers to Assyria and another entertained ambassadors from Babylon, but the whole history of the period implies frequent embassies of which no special mention is made, and one from the last king is dropped incidentally by Jeremiah with no record of it in the histories. Gill reports that Jarchi referred the coming of the Babylonians to those same ambassadors, gladly received by the king who showed them all the treasures of his house.

The alienation is explained politically. Ellicott says the original implies the disgust of satiety, and traces the vacillation: one king had been the devoted friend of Babylon and perished in his zeal for it, the kingdom was then made a dependency of Egypt and turned to Babylon for aid, and afterwards, taking the Babylonian yoke in turn, grew impatient of it and sought the aid of Egypt. At either turn, he says, the policy was so entirely wanting in sole reliance upon God as to produce the estrangement on the other side that the next verse records. Wesley puts it in five words, that she grew weary of the Chaldeans. Gill notes that the breach with the Babylonians ended nothing, since the people were rather more frequent and impudent in their idolatries afterwards and courted the friendship and worship of other nations, as a lewd woman who has cast off her former lovers does not leave her lewdness but seeks others; and that they went on increasing their alliances even while the Lord frowned upon them under the last two kings.

One word divides the voices. Gill renders it concubines and takes it of the neighbouring nations allied to Egypt, whose friendship the people courted and whose idols they served, adding that the Septuagint and Arabic versions wrongly read the Chaldeans here; Wesley agrees that the nations confederate with Egypt are meant. Clarke gives the same rendering of harlots or concubines but pauses on the English, noting that the word harlot anciently covered a prostitute of either sex. Ellicott insists the word is masculine, and takes it as indicating the abominable sins copied by the people from the heathen, with the asses and horses introduced to show the intensity of the lust. Gill closes the passage where it began, that in calling to remembrance the lewdness of her youth she committed the very idolatries her fathers had committed in Egypt, being now in alliance with the same people.
22:
Henry casts the passage as a criminal trial. The city stands indicted under her assumed name, as a false traitor to her sovereign Lord the God of heaven, who, not having his fear before her eyes but moved by the instigation of the devil, had revolted from her allegiance, compassed to shake off his government, and joined in confederacy with his enemies and the pretenders to a deity, in contempt of his crown and dignity. To this indictment she has pleaded not guilty, protesting that she is not polluted and has not gone after Baalim; but it is found against her by the notorious evidence of the fact, and she has nothing material to offer why judgment should not be given. What follows is the sentence, and its first article is that her old confederates must be her executioners. He notes that they are called her lovers here and, a few verses on, those whom she hates, and draws from it that sinful love soon turns to hatred, as with the son of David and his sister, since men of unreasonable passions are often as hot against what they were lately hot for. Ellicott makes the same correlation the point: she had chosen the idolatries of Egypt, Assyria and Babylon, and these drew down the vengeance of the one in whom alone was her refuge, so that the strength she sought in their alliance overwhelmed her with desolation.

Three names in the muster roll divide the voices. Wesley treats them as geography: one a province between two rivers in which old Nineveh stood, another a district containing the middle part of the kingdom of Babylon, the third bordering on Media. Ellicott grants our translators took them for proper names and that some still think them small Chaldean tribes, but holds it better, with the Vulgate and most modern commentators, to read them as titles of officers, rulers, lords and nobles, and he supports this from the renderings they receive elsewhere, crying and liberal and rich for one, visitation in a margin for another. Clarke surveys the field and refuses to settle it. The names have been thought to designate peoples bordering on the Chaldeans, but no geographer has found them; the old translations took them as appellatives, rulers and mighty men and tyrants; others render them literally as visiting, shouting and retreating; others apply them to the habits of the soldiery, the muster of armies, the magnificence of the uniform, the embroidery on the clothes of the captains; and one writer proposed three neighbouring nations. Clarke ends by saying he has nothing to add that would edify his readers.

The equipment and the mutilation are handled more soberly. Gill divides the train into chariots carrying the princes, wagons for provisions, and wheels either under them or carried spare against a breakage, and reports that some Jewish interpreters took the first word for warlike instruments in general; Wesley agrees about the spare wheels. Ellicott presses the same word, which occurs only here and is thought to mean a weapon, and would render it with weapons, chariots and wheels; he glosses the setting of judgment before them as an entrusting of the judgment to them, where Wesley reads a power of conquest over rebels together with a spirit of judgment to discern the greatness of the sin. On the cutting off of nose and ears both agree that this was an eastern punishment for adultery, Clarke citing a Latin epigram that asks who counselled the cutting off of an adulterous nose, and Ellicott that the custom of mutilating prisoners prevailed in the East from the earliest times and is named here with especial reference to destroying the attractiveness of the adulteress. Gill and Wesley read the jealousy as that of an enraged husband, and Gill closes with the outcome, that after this captivity the people were never guilty of idolatry again.
28:
The reversal is stated twice over. Gill notes that those to be delivered into are the very people before loved and doted upon and now hated and rebelled against, that falling into such hands must be a sore judgment, and that the threat is repeated in different words for the greater certainty of it. He adds that the hatred was mutual and returned in kind, the conquerors hating as much as they had been loved and as much as they were themselves hated, and showing it by putting some to the sword, carrying the rest captive and employing them in hard service; Wesley makes the taking away of their labour a deprivation of any comfortable use of it, since it would be exacted of them in captivity.

Gill raises a small textual point at the next verse. What the conquerors did God is said to do, because he suffered it as a punishment for their sins, and indeed it was according to his will and by his orders; but the Septuagint and the Vulgate render the clause in the third person instead, that they have done these things unto thee, meaning the conquerors themselves. He also marks the ground of the sentence, that the younger sister had walked in the way of the elder and was guilty of the very same idolatrous practices.

The cup is measured by each voice differently. Gill takes the drinking of it as partaking of the same punishment, very great, signified by a cup deep and large which holds much, and Clarke states it in a line, that she shall be ruined and desolated as her sister was. Ellicott adds the aggravation, that the cup of humiliation already drunk by the elder was large and filled with pain and sorrow, and yet the younger must drink it amid the derision of her neighbours. Wesley measures it by time, that the cup contains what will last many years, until the seventy be expired. Gill pairs the drunkenness with the sorrow that follows it, since the two generally go together and the one expresses the greatness of the other in captivity, and takes the sucking out as the very dregs at the bottom, the most nauseous and pernicious part, drunk not through love but by force.

The last gesture divides them. Clarke reads the plucking off of the breasts as a tearing, a frequent action in extreme sorrow and desolation along with weeping and beating the breast, and quotes a line of Ovid describing exactly that. Wesley reads it as self-inflicted vengeance, the woman revenging herself upon herself, and takes the breaking of the shards as an attempt to suck out whatever remains, with a staggering under sorrows that intoxicate and astonish. Gill and Wesley close the passage together, Gill taking the forgetting of God as a neglect of his word, worship and ordinances while strange gods were served, and Wesley dividing the bearing into two, the guilt which God will impute and the punishment which he will not pardon.
36:
The opening question is read as a question by some and as a command by others. Gill takes it as a question expecting no for an answer: wilt thou plead the cause of these two, say anything in their defence or excuse, or intercede and pray that the threatened judgments may not come upon them? Do nothing of the kind. Ellicott would drop the interrogative altogether and render it as an imperative, judge thou. Henry gives both readings in turn, first as a challenge whether the prophet will go about to frame an excuse for them, when the matter is so bad as not to bear one, and then, as he prefers, as a commission, that he shall now be employed in the name of God to judge them.

Henry also explains why the two are now taken together. After the ten tribes were carried away and their kingdom made desolate, what remained of them incorporated by degrees with the southern kingdom and many gained a settlement in the city, so that the two sisters had in effect become one again, and the prophet takes them to task jointly; and the matter, he adds, is rather worse than better since the union.

The charges are then set out in order. Henry lists three. The first and worst is gross idolatry, here called adultery, a breach of the marriage covenant with God and a lusting after the gratifications of a carnal and sensual mind in the very worship of God. The second is the most barbarous murder, the sacrificing of children, a sin so unnatural that they deserve to hear of it on all occasions, since innocent blood is on their hands, the blood of their own children; and Henry presses the wording, that they caused them to pass through the fire not that they might be dedicated to the idols but that they might be devoured, which shows that they loved their idols better than what was dearest to them in the world. Gill confirms the reading from the next verse, that causing the children to pass through the fire was a slaying of them and that their passing through it was for the idols and unto them. The third charge is the profaning of sacred things.

Whether the adultery is literal as well as figurative is left open. Gill allows both senses, either adultery with the wives of their neighbours, which he says was a prevailing sin with this people, or the spiritual adultery which is idolatry; Henry takes it wholly of idolatry. On the profaning, Clarke says shortly that they defiled the sanctuary by placing idols in it, and Wesley that when they had newly polluted themselves with idolatry and murder they thrust into the temple. Ellicott makes the timing carry the weight. The emphasis, he says, falls on their worshipping in the sanctuary the same day they offered their children to their idols, because passing directly from the one to the other showed an utter disregard of the commands of the Lord and an entire want of appreciation of his character and holiness. He adds a note on the manner of the passage, that the figure is here partly dropped so that the reality may come out better, which is why the language of these verses turns from the two sisters to the sanctuary and the sabbaths.
40:
Gill marks the direction of the traffic, that the heathen nations did not send to this people but this people to them, courting the alliance of Egypt, Assyria and Chaldea. Ellicott takes the figure as that of a lewd woman preparing for her paramour, and notes that painting the eyes, or rather the lids and lashes, was an ancient custom still preserved in the East. Clarke matches it with a modern parallel from a work on eastern customs, that this is how a loose woman in Bengal adorns herself to receive guests, bathing first, then painting about her eyes, then covering her body with ornaments.

The stately bed is read three ways. Gill allows either a throne under a canopy on which the king received ambassadors, or a couch at a feast, it being usual in eastern countries to sit on beds at meat; Ellicott settles on the couch or divan, and Wesley describes a bed on which women sat to feast while men leaned on their sides. Clarke reads it as an altar instead, raised to the idols, probably alluding to the one a king had made after the pattern he saw at Damascus, though he adds the sofas on which the ancients reclined at meals. On the incense and the oil Ellicott allows that they may be the products of the land bestowed on the heathen, but prefers to connect them with sacrifice, since both were especially used in it, so that what should have been the Lord alone was perverted to idols.

The next verse is the hardest in the chapter, and two voices rewrite it. Keil and Delitzsch call it very obscure and reject both the Latin rendering of a multitude exulting in her and the English of a careless multitude within her, since the word never means the voice of a multitude but a loud tumult; the adjective cannot qualify it, a quiet tumult being a contradiction, and must be the predicate, so that the loud noise became quiet. Ellicott reaches the same construction independently and supplies the sense: the tumult of the invading army was stilled by the gifts of the land, of which the history has frequent record. He goes further, denying that the word rendered as a people is a proper name and taking it for drunkards, placed in the wilderness not as their home but as the region they marched through; the sense being that the conquerors were satisfied with heavy tribute, and having received it gave themselves to drunkenness and decked out their tributary with ornaments. Gill and Wesley read the verse otherwise, as a welcome rather than an invasion, Gill taking the multitude either for the retinue of the ambassadors or for the people who came to see the public entry, and Wesley for a shout of joy over a treaty of peace. Clarke reads a third thing, an idolatrous festival at which a riotous multitude assembled and fellows of the baser sort performed the rites, with bracelets on their arms and garlands on their heads.

Two smaller corrections close the section. Ellicott would not make the following clause a question, nor the next verse adversative, but would render it as a statement, that now her whoredom shall be committed, the thought being that after all means of reclamation had failed God gave her up to her sins. He also explains the shifting number: the middle portion speaks throughout of the younger sister, the arraignment includes both though mostly in the singular because she was uppermost in the mind of the prophet, and the closing sentence returns to the plural, since although the elder had long since suffered it was important to show that a common sin involved both in a common punishment. Gill identifies the one old in adulteries as either sister, or as the whole people, addicted to idolatry ever since they came out of Egypt.
45:
Who the righteous men are gets four answers. Gill reports two before giving his own: some understand the prophets, really righteous men who foretold the righteous judgments of God upon an idolatrous people, and others righteous men in general, who would all agree that such crimes deserve the punishment usually inflicted on them; but he prefers the Babylonians, who, though not righteous in themselves, were so in comparison with a people that had a divine revelation and knew better, these being nations that knew neither God nor his will. Clarke names the same conquerors and gives the reason directly, that they are so called because appointed by God to execute judgment on these criminals. Ellicott defines the phrase rather than the persons, as men to whom the judgment of righteousness is committed. Wesley takes it at face value, of men who keep the law of their God.

The sentence itself mixes the figure with the fact. Ellicott says the two are designedly mixed here, since stoning was the legal punishment of adultery while the actual overthrow of the city was by the sword. Clarke keeps to the law, that they shall be stoned as adulteresses were under it, and Gill, having said the same, presses the historical side, that this seems to refer to the besieging army casting stones from their slings and engines into the city, killing some outright and beating down houses which fell upon others. Wesley identifies the company simply as the Babylonian army, and against the Jews as the children of the younger sister; Gill notes a variant in which the clause is not a promise but a command, the Targum representing the words as spoken to the prophet, that he should bring up a company against them.

The ceasing of the lewdness is read as an outcome and not only a threat. Gill takes it to mean that no opportunity for it was left and none left to commit it, since what the famine, sword and pestilence did not destroy during the siege was carried captive, and those who returned were never given to idolatry again. Clarke says the same more sweepingly, that from that time to his own day the people never relapsed into it, and Wesley that we read of none after the return from this captivity. Ellicott explains the mechanism differently, that the lewdness ceases by the removal of the sinners, and takes the phrase about all women, in keeping with the allegory, to mean all nations, so that the judgments should be then and for all time a conspicuous monument of the righteous severity of God. On the last verse Gill would render the recompensing as a giving of their lewdness, that is of its punishment, and Clarke and Ellicott agree, Ellicott glossing the bearing of the sins of their idols as bearing the punishment of the sins committed in worshipping them.
